topic: Cracking Wordle: Using Information Theory and Entropy
target_audience: University students (Computer Science or Data Science background)

outline.topic: Cracking Wordle: Using Information Theory and Entropy
outline.target_audience: University students (Computer Science or Data Science background)

sections.title: The Core Intuition: What is Information?
sections.content: Introduce the concept of 'Information Gain' as a reduction in uncertainty. Explain that a good guess isn't just about matching letters, but about narrowing down the search space (the set of possible remaining words).
sections.example: Imagine a secret animal behind a curtain. Asking 'Does it have fur?' vs 'Is it a platypus?' The first question provides more information by splitting the search space effectively.

sections.title: Quantifying Uncertainty: Entropy
sections.content: Define Shannon Entropy (H) mathematically. Explain that entropy represents the expected number of bits needed to represent the outcome. Visualize this as a probability distribution of remaining words; a uniform distribution (where many words are equally likely) has high entropy.
sections.example: A bar chart showing 100 possible words. If one guess leaves 50 words as candidates, entropy is high. If a guess leaves only 1, the uncertainty collapses to zero.

sections.title: The Optimal Guess Strategy
sections.content: Explain that the goal of every turn is to choose a word that maximizes the 'expected information gain' (i.e., minimizes the remaining entropy). We calculate the probability of every possible feedback pattern (Green, Yellow, Gray) and calculate the weighted average information gain.
sections.example: Visualizing a decision tree where a word like 'CRANE' splits the list of 2,309 English words into many smaller subsets, unlike a word like 'XYLYL' which leaves most words untouched.

sections.title: Interactive Demonstration
sections.content: Apply the logic to a concrete state. Show how selecting a word that creates balanced 'bins' of outcomes leads to the fastest resolution.
sections.example: A digital animation of a 'Robot Agent' solving Wordle: The robot considers the word 'SLATE'. The screen displays the branching paths (outcomes), highlighting how 'SLATE' splits the 2,309 words into the most balanced groups.

sections.title: Conclusion: Real-world Applications
sections.content: Summarize how information theory underpins modern technology beyond games. Connect entropy to data compression (ZIP files) and decision-tree algorithms in Machine Learning.
sections.example: Briefly show a ZIP file icon next to a Wordle grid, highlighting that both use entropy to optimize data storage and search efficiency.
